claim: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a global public health concern due to the rising myriad of hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant clones associated with high mortality.
source: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a global public health concern due to the rising myriad of hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant clones both alarmingly associated with high mortality.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references the clinical significance of K. pneumoniae, drawing on established knowledge about this pathogen.

claim: A total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the TraDIS experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transposon insertions in 11 genes decreased fitness for growth in urine.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental TraDIS data from urine growth experiments.

claim: Transposon insertions in 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in serum.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental TraDIS data from serum growth experiments.

claim: K. pneumoniae can colonize multiple body sites causing infections ranging from pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and bacteremia in immunocompromised patients and those with comorbidities.
source: In immunocompromised patients, and those with comorbidities such as diabetes or alcoholism, K. pneumoniae can colonize multiple body sites causing a diverse array of infections ranging from life-threatening pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and bacteremia (Ko et al., 2002; Gonçalves Barbosa et al., 2022; Tumbarello et al., 2015; Clegg and Murphy, 2016; Paczosa and Mecsas, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: K. pneumoniae is a frequently reported multidrug-resistant pathogen isolated from nosocomial settings.
source: K. pneumoniae is a frequently reported multidrug-resistant pathogen isolated from nosocomial settings.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about K. pneumoniae epidemiology.

claim: Infections with multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae have higher mortality rates and require longer treatment regimens and hospital stays.
source: Such infections have generally higher mortality rates and require longer treatment regimens and hospital stays, placing a significant burden on healthcare providers (GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022; Pham et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on antimicrobial resistance burden.

claim: Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in K. pneumoniae is mediated by horizontally acquired plasmid-mediated β-lactamases.
source: Of most concern is resistance to β-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin, aztreonam, and extended-spectrum cephalosporins, by horizontally acquired plasmid-mediated β-lactamases (Navon-Venezia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on antibiotic resistance mechanisms.

claim: Pandrug-resistant strains of K. pneumoniae have emerged.
source: While combined antibiotic therapies have been deployed in the clinic, the emergence of pandrug-resistant strains has created an urgency to develop new and efficient approaches to treat K. pneumoniae infections (Garbati and Al Godhair, 2013; Campos et al., 2016; Rojas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on pandrug-resistant K. pneumoniae.

claim: Distinct lineages of K. pneumoniae exist in clinical and environmental settings.
source: Recent large-scale phylogenetic investigations have suggested that distinct lineages of K. pneumoniae exist in clinical and environmental settings (Wyres et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published phylogenetic research.

claim: Two clinical pathotypes of K. pneumoniae have emerged: classical and hypervirulent.
source: Furthermore, two clinical pathotypes of K. pneumoniae have emerged: classical and hypervirulent.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about K. pneumoniae classification.

claim: Genes involved in adhesion, iron acquisition, capsulation, and cell envelope biogenesis are important for K. pneumoniae virulence.
source: While the full repertoire of genetic factors required for K. pneumoniae virulence remains unclear, various studies have highlighted the importance of genes involved in adhesion, iron acquisition, capsulation, and cell envelope biogenesis (Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on K. pneumoniae virulence factors.

claim: The ability to colonize the urinary tract and survive in the bloodstream are essential pathogenic traits for K. pneumoniae.
source: Nevertheless, for both classical and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains, the ability to colonize the urinary tract and survive in the bloodstream are essential pathogenic traits and are dependent on a large and diverse range of virulence factors (Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on K. pneumoniae pathogenesis.

claim: LPS O-antigens and capsular polysaccharide K-antigens contribute to serum resistance and antiphagocytosis in K. pneumoniae.
source: Indeed, previous studies demonstrated that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (O-) (9 serotypes) and capsular polysaccharide (cps) (K-) antigens (79 serotypes) contribute to the resistance of serum-mediated killing and antiphagocytosis (Choi et al., 2020; Martin and Bachman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on K. pneumoniae surface antigens.

claim: Serum resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is defined by a multitude of factors (the serum resistome).
source: However, prior genetic screens have revealed that serum resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is an intricate phenotype defined by a multitude of factors (the serum resistome) (Short et al., 2020; Phan et al., 2013; McCarthy and Taylor, 2022; Ondari et al., 2019; Subashchandrabose et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on serum resistance.

claim: A recent study identified 93 different genes associated with serum resistance across four K. pneumoniae strains, with only three genes (lpp, arnD, and rfaH) playing a role in all strains.
source: A recent study of K. pneumoniae identified 93 different genes associated with serum resistance across four distinct strains but found that only three genes (lpp, arnD, and rfaH) played a role in all strains.
evidence: This claim references findings from a recent published study on K. pneumoniae serum resistance.

claim: Multiple mechanisms of serum resistance may exist in Klebsiella lineages.
source: These data hint that multiple mechanisms of serum resistance may exist in Klebsiella lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of variable serum resistance genes across strains.

claim: The full repertoire of genes required for growth of K. pneumoniae in the urinary tract (the urinome) has not been defined.
source: In contrast, the full repertoire of genes required for growth of K. pneumoniae in the urinary tract (the urinome) has not been defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: K. pneumoniae ECL8 is a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage.
source: In this study, we generated a highly saturated transposon library within K. pneumoniae ECL8, a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage that includes hypervirulent clones of epidemiological significance known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia (Hoashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the strain used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: K2-ST375 includes hypervirulent clones known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia.
source: In this study, we generated a highly saturated transposon library within K. pneumoniae ECL8, a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage that includes hypervirulent clones of epidemiological significance known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia (Hoashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on K2-ST375 epidemiology.

claim: A K. pneumoniae ECL8 mini-Tn5 mutant library composed of >1 million mutants was constructed.
source: A K. pneumoniae ECL8 mini-Tn5 mutant library composed of >1 million mutants was constructed and subsequently subjected to TraDIS.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methodology and library construction.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 reference genome consists of an ~5.3 Mb chromosome and a single 205 kb plasmid.
source: The resulting reads were mapped to the reference genome that consists of an ~5.3 Mb chromosome and a single 205 kb plasmid (EMBL Accessions: HF536482.1 and HF536483) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by reference to the genome sequence and Figure 1.

claim: The gene insertion index scores (IIS) of the two technical replicates of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library (KTL1 and KTL2) were highly correlated with each other (R2=0.955).
source: The gene insertion index scores (IIS) of the two technical replicates of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library (KTL1 and KTL2) were highly correlated with each other (R2=0.955), demonstrating a high level of reproducibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites.
source: This library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites and 499,919 of these insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequencing data results.

claim: 499,919 transposon insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries in the K. pneumoniae ECL8 library.
source: This library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites and 499,919 of these insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the sequencing data results.

claim: The transposon coverage equates to an average transposon insertion every 9.93 bp throughout the genome.
source: This high level of transposon coverage equates to an average transposon insertion every 9.93 bp throughout the genome, equivalent to an insertion approximately every four codons.
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data.

claim: The plasmid is likely present as a single copy in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: A de Brujin graph visualized in the genome assembly package Bandage revealed that the sequencing coverage of the plasmid was only 1.33-fold higher than that of the chromosome indicating that the plasmid is likely present as a single copy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Wick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing coverage analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 373 chromosomal genes were classified as essential for growth on solid LB medium supplemented with kanamycin.
source: Based on the above criteria, 373 chromosomal genes were assigned a log2-LR of less than –3.6 and were therefore classified as essential for growth on solid Luria-Bertani (LB) medium supplemented with kanamycin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: Most genes (4551) were classified as non-essential.
source: Most genes (4551) were classified as non-essential (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: A subset of 241 genes were located between the essential and non-essential modes with their essentiality mode being deemed 'unclear'.
source: A subset of 241 genes were located between these two modes with their essentiality mode being deemed 'unclear' (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: No essential genes were identified within the COG categories for chromatin structure and dynamics (B), cell motility (N), and secondary structure (Q).
source: We identified no essential genes within the COG categories for chromatin structure and dynamics (B), cell motility (N), and secondary structure (Q) suggesting genes within these categories are not required or redundant for K. pneumoniae growth in the utilized nutrient-rich liquid medium.
evidence: This is based on COG enrichment analysis of the essential genes.

claim: Genes involved in signal transduction (T) and inorganic ion transport/metabolism (P) were depleted among essential genes.
source: However, genes involved in signal transduction (T) and inorganic ion transport/metabolism (P) were depleted, while genes involved in translation (J), cell cycle control (D), and co-enzyme metabolism (H) were the most highly enriched.
evidence: This is based on COG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genes involved in translation (J), cell cycle control (D), and co-enzyme metabolism (H) were the most highly enriched among essential genes.
source: However, genes involved in signal transduction (T) and inorganic ion transport/metabolism (P) were depleted, while genes involved in translation (J), cell cycle control (D), and co-enzyme metabolism (H) were the most highly enriched.
evidence: This is based on COG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The enriched COG categories among essential genes in K. pneumoniae ECL8 correlate with those in other Proteobacteria such as Salmonella enterica Typhimurium, S. enterica Typhi, and Caulobacter crescentus.
source: This correlates with enriched COG categories shared among essential genes in other members of the Proteobacteria such as Salmonella enterica Typhimurium, S. enterica Typhi, and Caulobacter crescentus and serves as an internal control for the validity of the library (Christen et al., 2011; Grazziotin et al., 2015; Barquist et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on essential genes in other bacteria.

claim: 11 genes on the K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid met the criteria to be defined as essential.
source: The identification of 11 genes on the K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid that met the criteria to be defined as essential was an unexpected observation (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data for plasmid genes.

claim: The bacterial copy number of the plasmid was approximated to be one.
source: As previously noted, the bacterial copy number of the plasmid was approximated to be one.
evidence: This is based on the sequencing coverage analysis mentioned earlier.

claim: The 11 plasmid-borne 'essential' genes included repB, which is required for plasmid replication.
source: Notably, the 11 plasmid-borne 'essential' genes included repB, which is required for plasmid replication.
evidence: This is based on the identification of repB among the plasmid essential genes and knowledge of its function.

claim: The 11 plasmid genes are likely to be required for plasmid replication and stability and are unlikely to be essential for growth.
source: Therefore, these genes are likely to be required for plasmid replication and stability and are unlikely to be essential for growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of repB and the observation that K. pneumoniae can survive without plasmids.

claim: K. pneumoniae remains viable when large indigenous virulence plasmids are cured from the bacterium.
source: This hypothesis is supported by previous observations that K. pneumoniae remains viable when large indigenous virulence plasmids are cured from the bacterium (Tang et al., 2010; Rodríguez-Medina et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on plasmid curing experiments.

claim: A total of 667 genomic regions with insertion-free regions (IFRs) ≥145 bp were identified.
source: A total of 667 genomic regions with IFRs≥145 bp were identified, many which correspond to the 380 essential genes identified through the bimodal analysis described earlier.
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: An insertion-free region (IFR) of 145 bp or greater was statistically significant for the K. pneumoniae ECL8 library.
source: This model indicated that with the insertion frequency calculated for this library, for a genome of 5.3 Mb, an insertion-free region (IFR) of 145 bp or greater was statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on a geometric model applied to the TraDIS data.

claim: The polA gene contained an 826 bp IFR corresponding to 275 amino acids predicted to encode the 5'–3' exonuclease function of the protein.
source: For example, the polA gene was classified as 'unclear' but contained, barring a single transposon insertion event, an 826 bp IFR. This IFR corresponds to 275 amino acids that are predicted to encode the 5'–3' exonuclease function of the protein (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis and protein domain prediction.

claim: The 5'–3' exonuclease region of polA has been shown to be required for the growth of Escherichia coli in laboratory conditions.
source: This region has also been shown to be required for the growth of Escherichia coli in laboratory conditions (Joyce and Grindley, 1984; Gallagher et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on E. coli polA.

claim: 54 additional genes with statistically significant IFRs were identified aside from those already identified by the bimodal analyses.
source: Aside from those genes already identified by the bimodal analyses described above, our analyses revealed 54 additional genes with statistically significant IFRs, which indicates that they are likely essential for growth under the conditions tested here.
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: K. pneumoniae ECL8 contains at least 427 essential genes.
source: Thus, our data suggest K. pneumoniae contains at least 427 essential genes, which we define as the ECL8 curated essential gene list.
evidence: This is based on combining the bimodal analysis (373 genes) and IFR analysis (54 additional genes).

claim: 59 regions ≥145 bp lacked transposon insertion sites and did not map to within annotated CDS boundaries.
source: Interestingly, the methodology used here revealed 59 regions ≥145 bp that lacked transposon insertion sites and did not map to within annotated CDS boundaries (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: 46 of the 59 unannotated IFR regions contain potential ORFs that could encode proteins through blastX identification.
source: Forty-six of these regions contain potential ORFs that could encode proteins through blastX identification.
evidence: This is based on blastX analysis of the unannotated IFR regions.

claim: TraDIS datasets have untapped potential to identify previously uncharacterized, essential, small CDSs, and promoter elements.
source: This study emphasizes the untapped potential of TraDIS datasets to identify previously uncharacterized, essential, small CDSs, and promoter elements that are not immediately obvious by traditional and computational genomic annotation methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the identification of unannotated IFRs.

claim: Transcription of polycistronic operons can be affected by the insertion orientation of the transposon.
source: As reported previously (Goodall et al., 2018; Hutchison et al., 2019), due to the design of the transposon used in this study, transcription of polycistronic operons can be affected by the insertion orientation of the transposon (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Directional insertion bias of the transposon was noted within the cps operon encoding the K2 capsule.
source: Directional insertion bias of the transposon was noted within a large genomic region of ~14 kb encoding the virulence-associated cps operon (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of transposon insertion patterns shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 cps operon encodes for a KL2/K2 capsule with 18/18 of the expected genes.
source: The bioinformatic webtool 'Kaptive' determined with high confidence the K. pneumoniae ECL8 cps operon encodes for a KL2/K2 capsule with 18/18 of the expected genes (Figure 7—source data 1; Lam et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on Kaptive analysis of the genome sequence.

claim: Transposon insertions were poorly tolerated in the forward Tn orientation of the DNA strand in the cps operon.
source: Notably, transposon insertions were poorly tolerated in the forward Tn orientation of the DNA strand.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of transposon insertion patterns shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of essential genes among four K. pneumoniae strains (ECL8, KPNIH1, RH201207, ATCC 43816) ranged from 434 to 642.
source: The number of essential genes among the four strains ranged from 434 to 642; a complete list and comparison of our curated gene list against the reported gene lists of KPNIH1, RH201207, and ATCC 43816 is found in Figure 3—source data 1.
evidence: This is based on comparison of essential gene lists from different studies.

claim: The higher number of essential genes predicted in the KPNIH1 gene list may be due to a lower transposon density.
source: We speculate that the higher number of essential genes predicted in the KPNIH1 gene list is due to a lower transposon density, as this is associated with an increased likelihood of false-positive results (Chao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the relationship between library density and false-positive rates, supported by a citation.

claim: 57% of the essential genes identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8 were essential in the other three strains (KPNIH1, RH201207, ATCC 43816).
source: While further validation experiments will be required to determine whether specific genes are essential, 57% of the essential genes identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8 were essential in the other three strains.
evidence: This is based on comparison of essential gene lists from different studies.

claim: Ten genes that satisfied a stringent threshold of a log2 fold change (log2FC)>–2 and a Q-value≤0.05 were considered as advantageous for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine.
source: Ten genes that satisfied a stringent threshold of a log2 fold change (log2FC)>–2 and a Q-value≤0.05, relative to the LB control, were considered as advantageous for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.

claim: Genes advantageous for growth in urine included those encoding SodA, OmpA, Skp, and proteins associated with iron acquisition (fepB, fepD, fepG, exbB, and exbD).
source: These included genes encoding the superoxide dismutase SodA, the structural outer membrane protein OmpA (Pain et al., 2015), the periplasmic chaperone Skp (Mas et al., 2019), and five proteins (fepB, fepD, fepG, exbB, and exbD) associated with iron acquisition (Caza and Kronstad, 2013).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine and supported by citations.

claim: The remaining two genes advantageous for growth in urine (ytfL and argH) play key roles in controlling cytoplasmic cadaverine and putrescine concentrations and amino acid biosynthesis.
source: The remaining two genes (ytfL and argH) play key roles in controlling cytoplasmic cadaverine and putrescine concentrations and amino acid biosynthesis, respectively (Iwadate et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis and supported by citations to published literature on gene function.

claim: The ΔsodA::aph mutant was less fit in both urine and LB, but the phenotype was exacerbated in urine.
source: When compared to the WT, a ΔsodA::aph mutant was less fit in both urine and LB, but the phenotype was exacerbated in urine.
evidence: This is based on competitive index experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The fitness of the ΔompA, ΔfepB, ΔfepD, ΔexbB, and ΔexbD mutants was comparable to the parent strain when grown in LB medium and only less fit when grown in urine.
source: In contrast, the fitness of the remaining mutants was comparable to the parent strain when grown in LB medium and only less fit when grown in urine.
evidence: This is based on competitive index experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ompA, fepB, fepD, exbB, and exbD mutants were dramatically less fit than the parent strain in urine.
source: While the relative competitive index of the ΔytfL::aph strain was 0.8 in urine, the ompA, fepB, fepD, exbB, and exbD mutants were dramatically less fit than the parent strain in urine (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on competitive index experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Iron levels were limiting growth in human urine.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesized that iron levels were limiting growth in human urine and that the ability to acquire iron was crucial for K. pneumoniae to survive and grow in vivo (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Banerjee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that iron acquisition genes are required for growth in urine, supported by citations.

claim: The optical density of K. pneumoniae cultures decreased after passage in urine.
source: However, the optical density of K. pneumoniae cultures decreased after passage in urine (Figure 5B), and the restricted growth was further exacerbated by the addition of the iron chelator 2,2-dipyridyl (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on growth experiments shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Supplementation of urine with exogenous iron increased growth relative to non-supplemented cultures.
source: In contrast, supplementation of urine with exogenous iron increased growth relative to non-supplemented cultures with no difference in growth upon passage (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on growth experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mutants lacking genes involved in iron uptake (fepB, fepD, exbB, exbD) were drastically less fit than the WT in urine.
source: Not unexpectedly, area under the curve analysis revealed that mutants lacking genes involved in iron uptake (fepB, fepD, exbB, exbD) were drastically less fit than the WT (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on growth curve analysis shown in Figure 5E (note: text says Figure 6E but should be Figure 5E based on context).

claim: The highest log2FC increase (~7-fold) in read counts mapped to the Ferric Uptake Regulator (fur) gene indicating its loss is beneficial for growth in urine.
source: In contrast, the highest log2FC increase (~7-fold) in read counts mapped to the Ferric Uptake Regulator (fur) gene indicating its loss is beneficial for growth in urine.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.

claim: The Fur regulon plays a pivotal role for K. pneumoniae growth in urine by tightly regulating enterobactin synthesis and enterobactin-mediated iron uptake.
source: Altogether, this suggests that the Fur regulon plays a pivotal role for K. pneumoniae growth in urine by tightly regulating enterobactin synthesis and enterobactin-mediated iron uptake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TraDIS data showing enrichment of fur mutants and decreased fitness of fep mutants.

claim: A 2 log10 decrease in the number of viable K. pneumoniae cells was observed after 90 min exposure to normal human serum.
source: In contrast, a 2 log10 decrease in the number of viable K. pneumoniae cells was observed after 90 min exposure to normal human serum, and a >4 log10 decrease after 180 min exposure.
evidence: This is based on serum killing kinetics experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A >4 log10 decrease in viable K. pneumoniae cells was observed after 180 min exposure to normal human serum.
source: In contrast, a 2 log10 decrease in the number of viable K. pneumoniae cells was observed after 90 min exposure to normal human serum, and a >4 log10 decrease after 180 min exposure.
evidence: This is based on serum killing kinetics experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No reduction in viable K. pneumoniae cells was noted in heat-inactivated serum control.
source: To determine whether the observed reduction in viable cells was due to the presence of active complement proteins, K. pneumoniae was incubated in heat-inactivated serum control where no reduction in viable was noted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on serum killing kinetics experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 356 genes with a log2FC≤–2, p<0.05, and Q-value of ≤0.05 between the serum and heat-inactivated control were classified as genes that are advantageous for growth under complement-mediated killing conditions.
source: A total of 356 genes with a log2FC≤–2, p<0.05, and Q-value of ≤0.05 between the serum and heat-inactivated control were classified as genes that are advantageous for growth under complement-mediated killing conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum.

claim: The operons encoding LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis contained several conditionally essential genes for serum resistance.
source: The operons encoding LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis were noted as containing several conditionally essential genes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutants defective in LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis have been reported to play a role in membrane integrity and resistance to serum killing for a variety of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Mutants defective in these cell envelope structures have previously been reported to play a role in membrane integrity and resistance to serum killing for a variety of Gram-negative bacteria (Onsare et al., 2015; Salamon et al., 2020; Rai and Mitchell, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on serum resistance mechanisms.

claim: Genes implicated as important for serum resistance include GalE, MlaA, ClsA, BamE, LpxC, and YejM.
source: Genes implicated as important for serum resistance encode proteins with an important role in membrane stability. They include GalE involved in LPS sugar subunit biosynthesis (Frirdich and Whitfield, 2005; Ramos et al., 2012), outer membrane protein MlaA involved in phospholipid retrograde transport (Yeow et al., 2018), cardiolipin synthase ClsA (Tan et al., 2012), Bam complex component BamE (Rigel et al., 2012), and proteins involved in LPS biosynthesis (LpxC) and its regulator (YejM) (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis and supported by citations to published literature on gene function.

claim: The putative glycosyltransferase wbbY had the greatest log2FC decrease between serum and a heat-inactivated control.
source: To validate our observations, we selected the gene with the greatest log2FC decrease between serum and a heat-inactivated control, a putative glycosyltransferase espE_3/wbbY (inset, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ECL8 encodes the O-antigen serotype O1v2 with the operon having 98.98% nucleotide identity to the reference genome.
source: Analyses using the 'Kaptive' webtool suggested that ECL8 encodes the O-antigen serotype O1v2 with the operon having 98.98% nucleotide identity to the reference genome (Figure 7—source data 1; Lam et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on Kaptive analysis of the genome sequence.

claim: The O-antigen of the O1v2 serotype features distal repeating D-galactan I and D-galactan II sugar subunits.
source: The O-antigen of the O1v2 serotype features distal repeating D-galactan I and D-galactan II sugar subunits (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on O-antigen structure.

claim: A comparable growth profile was observed for K. pneumoniae ECL8 and the ΔwbbY::aph mutant in LB medium.
source: A comparable growth profile was observed for K. pneumoniae ECL8 and the ΔwbbY::aph mutant in LB medium (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on growth curve experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The ΔwbbY::aph mutant was more sensitive to human serum than the parent with no viable mutants surviving after 30 min.
source: However, the ΔwbbY::aph mutant was more sensitive to human serum than the parent with no viable mutants surviving after 30 min (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on serum killing assay experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ΔwbbY::aph strain produced LPS with a lower molecular weight compared to the parent strain.
source: The ΔwbbY::aph strain produced LPS with a lower molecular weight compared to the parent strain, suggesting that a truncated O-antigen was expressed.
evidence: This is based on LPS profile analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Alterations in the amount or length of LPS produced are known to influence susceptibility to serum-mediated killing.
source: Alterations in the amount or length of LPS produced are known to influence susceptibility to serum-mediated killing (Salamon et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on LPS and serum resistance.

claim: Deletion of wbbY in K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 (ST23) resulted in LPS profile defects due to abrogated D-galactan II production.
source: Importantly, Hsieh et al. have previously reported that deletion by wbbY in K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 (ST23) resulted in LPS profile defects due to abrogated D-galactan II production (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on wbbY function.

claim: Gene complementation of wbbY restores LPS profiles and serum resistance in K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044.
source: The authors also demonstrate that gene complementation restores LPS profiles and serum resistance, thus demonstrating that this screen was robust in identifying a key K. pneumoniae gene involved in complement-mediated killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to published literature on wbbY complementation.

claim: Mutation of five genes (ompA, galE, exbB, exbD, and sodA) conferred reduced fitness for both growth in urine and survival in serum.
source: Despite the intra- and interspecies variation in the serum resistome noted above, comparison of the urinome and serum resistome of K. pneumoniae ECL8 revealed that mutation of five genes (ompA, galE, exbB, exbD, and sodA) conferred reduced fitness for both growth in urine and survival in serum.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the TraDIS data from urine and serum experiments.

claim: A role for OmpA in serum resistance has previously been described for E. coli.
source: Notably, a role for OmpA in serum resistance has previously been described for E. coli, however it was not identified by TraDIS experiments investigating the serum resistome (Phan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on OmpA and serum resistance.

claim: GalE plays a key role in serum resistance for E. coli and Salmonella spp.
source: GalE is known to play a key role in serum resistance for E. coli and Salmonella spp.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about GalE function.

claim: GalE encodes a UDP-glucose 4-epimerase catalyzing the interconversion of UDP-D-galactose/UDP-D-glucose.
source: The gene galE encodes a UDP-glucose 4-epimerase catalyzing the interconversion of UDP-D-galactose/UDP-D-glucose (Frirdich and Whitfield, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on GalE function.

claim: GalE plays a role in D-galactan II synthesis, an O1 LPS component in K. pneumoniae.
source: It has been previously reported that GalE plays a role in D-galactan II synthesis, an O1 LPS component in K. pneumoniae (Ramos et al., 2012; Clarke and Whitfield, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on GalE and LPS biosynthesis.

claim: Loss of galE results in a modified LPS in K. pneumoniae resulting in increased serum susceptibility.
source: These data suggest that loss of galE results in a modified LPS in K. pneumoniae resulting in increased serum susceptibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TraDIS data and knowledge of GalE function.

claim: SodA converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen to prevent DNA and other cellular damage.
source: Additionally, the manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase SodA converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen to prevent DNA and other cellular damage (Touati, 1983; Doukyu and Taguchi, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on SodA function.

claim: A previous study in K. pneumoniae has reported the inducible expression of sodA in a triumvirate system with sodB and sodC.
source: A previous study in K. pneumoniae has reported the inducible expression of sodA in a triumvirate system with sodB and sodC, expressed in response to anaerobic challenge and high-oxygen concentration (Najmuldeen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on sodA regulation.

claim: The importance of sodA might be a consequence of elevated levels of reactive oxygen species due to iron acquisition.
source: Hence, the observed importance of sodA might be a consequence of elevated levels of reactive oxygen species due to iron acquisition and could represent a specialized metabolic adaptation for growth in these environments.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that sodA is required in both urine and serum.

claim: These findings underline the interplay between bacterial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Ultimately, these findings underline the interplay between bacterial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress previously reported in Gram-negative bacteria (Cornelis et al., 2011; Adler et al., 2014; Peralta et al., 2016; Guest et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on iron homeostasis and oxidative stress.

claim: Transposon insertion orientation bias into gnd was observed.
source: An interesting finding was the observed transposon insertion orientation bias into gnd.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of transposon insertion patterns shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The downstream transcriptional unit of gnd are O-antigen-related genes.
source: As the downstream transcriptional unit of gnd are O-antigen-related genes (i.e. biosynthesis and export), this in turn lends further credence to a transcriptional regulatory model where biosynthesis of O-antigen and capsule is coupled for biophysical reasons as has been previously reported (Dorman et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on the genomic context of gnd and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: O-antigen biosynthesis genes (wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance.
source: Collectively, these data show that O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance while hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than WT K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum.

claim: hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than WT K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Collectively, these data show that O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance while hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than WT K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis and validation experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: At 30 min post-incubation the number of viable hns::aph cells was decreased by ~2 log.
source: At 30 min post-incubation the number of viable hns::aph cells was decreased by ~2 log. However, no additional decrease in viable cell numbers was observed at later time points and these strains proliferated in serum (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on serum killing assay experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: hns::aph strains proliferated in serum after 30 min.
source: At 30 min post-incubation the number of viable hns::aph cells was decreased by ~2 log. However, no additional decrease in viable cell numbers was observed at later time points and these strains proliferated in serum (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on serum killing assay experiments shown in Figure 7F.

claim: rcsA, galF, wzi, and manC were derepressed in a Δhns K. pneumoniae mutant resulting in increased capsule production.
source: Ares and colleagues demonstrated that rcsA; galF; wzi; and manC were derepressed in a Δhns K. pneumoniae mutant resulting in increased capsule production (Ares et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on hns regulation.

claim: Upregulation of rcsA was noted in an E. coli Δhns mutant.
source: Similarly, upregulation of rcsA was noted in an E. coli Δhns mutant.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about hns regulation in E. coli.

claim: RcsA is known to positively regulate the capsular locus.
source: RcsA is known to positively regulate the capsular locus (Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1995; Ebel and Trempy, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on RcsA function.

claim: IgaA represses the Rcs regulon, preventing activation of RcsA.
source: Notably, IgaA represses the Rcs regulon, preventing activation of RcsA.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about IgaA function.

claim: Mutants in igaA are enriched in the serum resistance experiments.
source: Mutants in igaA are enriched in our experiments (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Activation of the Rcs regulon confers resistance to serum killing in K. pneumoniae by increasing capsule production.
source: These data suggest that activation of the Rcs regulon confers resistance to serum killing in K. pneumoniae, as noted for other members of the Enterobacteriaceae, by increasing capsule production (Meng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the TraDIS data and supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: This is the first report of a role for hns in resisting complement-mediated killing in human serum.
source: Despite the previously described links between hns and the regulation of a selection of capsular genes (Dorman et al., 2018; Ares et al., 2016), this is the first report of a role for hns in resisting complement-mediated killing in human serum.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the observation, supported by comparison to previous studies.

claim: The defined ECL8 urinome and serum resistome gene sets from this study differ from other TraDIS studies.
source: The defined ECL8 urinome and serum resistome gene sets from this study differ from other TraDIS studies, hinting that the genotype of different pathogenic lineages might only be a piece in understanding the underlying infection biology.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the results to other published studies.

claim: The genotype of different pathogenic lineages might only be a piece in understanding the underlying infection biology.
source: The defined ECL8 urinome and serum resistome gene sets from this study differ from other TraDIS studies, hinting that the genotype of different pathogenic lineages might only be a piece in understanding the underlying infection biology.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of variation in fitness genes across strains.

claim: The library was sequenced to near saturation as the discovery of unique reads plateaued at ~2 million reads.
source: Through iterative rounds of sequencing, we determined that the library was sequenced to near saturation as the discovery of unique reads plateaued at ~2 million reads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the saturation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average IIS of a gene located on the plasmid and the chromosome was comparable, 0.16 and 0.11, respectively.
source: The average IIS of a gene located on the plasmid and the chromosome was comparable, 0.16 and 0.11, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: The gene IISs for the library passaged in both LB and urine were highly correlated with respective biological replicates of 0.8483 and 0.9078 R2.
source: As the gene IISs for the library passaged in both LB and urine were highly correlated with respective biological replicates of 0.8483 and 0.9078 R2, replicates were combined for downstream analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient (R2) of gene IIS for two sequenced biological replicates were calculated as 0.91 (normal human serum) and 0.76 (heat-inactivated serum).
source: The Pearson correlation coefficient (R2) of gene IIS for two sequenced biological replicates were calculated as 0.91 (normal human serum) and 0.76 (heat-inactivated serum) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A recent study identified 93 different genes associated with serum resistance across four K. pneumoniae strains.
source: While that study found 93 genes that were required for survival in one or more strains, remarkably only three genes were common to all four strains: rfaH, lpp, and arnD.
evidence: This claim references findings from a recent published study on K. pneumoniae serum resistance.

claim: Comparison of the ECL8 serum resistome with the 56 genes comprising the serum resistome of E. coli strain EC958 revealed 14 genes in common.
source: Surprisingly, comparison of our data with the 56 genes comprising the serum resistome of the more distantly related multidrug-resistant E. coli strain EC958 revealed 14 genes in common.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the TraDIS data to published E. coli data.

claim: In all cases the genes encoding O-antigen and/or capsule synthesis were required for growth in normal human serum.
source: First, in all cases the genes encoding O-antigen and/or capsule synthesis were required for growth in normal human serum.
evidence: This is a generalization based on comparison of multiple serum resistome studies.

claim: arnD was not required for serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Comparison with our dataset revealed that in contrast to rfaH, arnD was not required for serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum.

claim: lpp is required for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in human serum but not resistance to complement-dependent killing per se.
source: A case in point is the lpp gene. This observation indicates that lpp is required for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in human serum but not resistance to complement-dependent killing per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lpp had fewer than 50 insertions in the heat-inactivated serum control.

claim: The study utilized filter sterilized urine which may preclude identification of genes required for interspecies interactions in the urinary microbiome.
source: It should be mentioned, our study utilized filter sterilized urine which may preclude identification of genes that are required for interspecies predation, cross-protection, and cross-feeding in the context of a urinary microbiome (Mataigne et al., 2021; Goh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a limitation of the study methodology, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The serum resistome of K. pneumoniae ECL8 consisted of more than 144 genes.
source: In contrast to the limited number of genes in the urinome, the serum resistome consisted of more than 144 genes.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum.

claim: The urinome of K. pneumoniae ECL8 consisted of only 11 genes.
source: Unexpectedly, our study revealed only 11 genes significantly required for growth in urine.
evidence: This is based on the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.
